title: Why read him anyway
hook: a flawed man who wrote the most human Stoic letters

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nero's tutor, years at the heart of a dangerous court. Your line was hard compromises. Did you catch yourself going along with something? Day four hundred ninety-three.

After the last two days, a fair question. Why have we spent sixty-some lessons with this man? A rich man who praised poverty. An adviser who stayed close to a murderer. We could have spent the whole season with Epictetus, a former slave who owned almost nothing, or Marcus Aurelius, who at least ran the empire himself. And yet readers keep coming back to Seneca, for nearly two thousand years, and not in spite of his flaws exactly. Partly because of them. Today: why read him anyway.
screen: `A RICH MAN WHO PRAISED POVERTY.` → `AN ADVISER TO A MURDERER.` → `TWO THOUSAND YEARS OF READERS.`

segments.voice: First, he admits things. Seneca tells Lucilius he got seasick and jumped overboard. That he wept too much for a friend. That he's not wise. Epictetus teaches from the front of the room. Seneca writes from the next seat over, struggling with the same lesson. Second, he lived where most of us live. Not in a cave, not on a throne. In the middle: money, family, a job that asked things of him he didn't like. His letters are written from inside compromise, which is where most readers are standing too. Third, readers in every age. Some early Christian writers loved him so much that a set of letters between Seneca and the apostle Paul was forged and passed around for centuries. The writer Tertullian called him often one of ours. The French essayist Montaigne, fifteen hundred years later, said Seneca and Plutarch were the books he returned to most. People from very different paths found a friend in him. Fourth, how he died. In 65, ordered by Nero to end his life, Seneca turned to his friends. Tacitus says he told them that since he couldn't leave them gifts, he would leave the one thing he had, and the finest: the image of his life. Paulina tried to die with him; Nero's soldiers saved her, and she lived on for some years. An image with stains on it. That may be exactly why it teaches. A perfect man would be easy to admire and hard to learn from.
screen: `HE ADMITS THINGS.` · `HE LIVED IN THE MIDDLE, LIKE US.` · `PAUL, TERTULLIAN, MONTAIGNE.` · `THE IMAGE OF HIS LIFE.` · then, large: `FLAWED AND WISE.`

segments.voice: Of everything Seneca wrote in these sixty-some days, which line has stayed with you? Hold every hour. Who is poor. The dark is in me. Like the bees. Rich in enough. Let one rise up without forcing it. Now ask why that one. What in your life did it touch? If it helps, picture him at his desk, an imperfect man, writing it for a friend. Then picture yourself, also imperfect, reading it. The bell holds the time.
Why read him anyway. Because he admits his faults, writes from the middle of a compromised life, and left his friends the image of it, stains and all. Today's word.
Your line: flawed and wise. Write down the one Seneca line you chose and keep it where you'll find it again. A wallet, a bookmark, the back of your phone case. Day four hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Many readers of Seneca keep a favorite letter or line to reread over the years, and read him alongside the honest record of his life rather than as a flawless sage.

fork.setup: you're Seneca, ordered to die, with friends around you and nothing you're allowed to give them. what do you leave?
fork.reveal: Tacitus says he left them the one thing he had, and the finest: the image of his life.

original.note: Latin, 'the image of a life': what Tacitus says Seneca left his friends.

trapdoor: what you thought: a flawed teacher can't teach you anything.
what it means: Seneca's faults put him in the middle of life, where most readers are, and he admits them.
what a scholar hears: the forged Seneca–Paul correspondence was known to Jerome in the 4th century, which helped keep Seneca on Christian reading lists through the Middle Ages.

notes: Tacitus, Annals 15.62: Seneca leaves friends 'imaginem vitae suae', the one and finest thing he had; 15.63–64 Paulina's attempt and survival 'for a few years'. Confirm.
Tertullian, De Anima 20: 'Seneca saepe noster'. Confirm.
Montaigne, Essays 2.10: names Plutarch and Seneca as his favorites. Confirm.
The Seneca–Paul correspondence (14 letters) is a later forgery; Jerome, De viris illustribus 12, mentions it. Confirm.
Back-references (seasick, wept too much, 'I am not wise') point to days 465, 469, and ahead to day 510; 'not wise' is mentioned briefly here.
